14.1.l: Arthroplasty — Patella Baja, Stiffness & Periprosthetic Fractures
14.1.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is patella baja after TKA and how do you treat it?"
- "Low patella **relative to the joint line** → hits the insert in flexion → pain, maltracking."
- "**Truly short tendon** (scar, earlier surgery) vs **apparent baja** (raised joint line, low button)."
- "Release → lower the joint line → **tibial tubercle proximalisation** → patellectomy last."

### Assessment & features
- Judge height against the **joint line**, not the tubercle
- After TKA → **tendon contracture** + joint line raised relative to the tubercle (Campbell)
- Low patella strikes the **tibial insert** in flexion → anterior pain, less flexion
- Indices → Insall–Salvati <0.8 · after TKA **Blackburne–Peel** and joint-line landmarks → chapter 12
[[FIG: Fig 14.1 · 14.1

### Causes
- **Congenital** · short tendon → hard to fix · apparent baja → avoidable at TKA
- Scar after **opening wedge HTO** (high tibial osteotomy), **tubercle distalisation**, **tendon repair**
- After osteotomy → immobilisation, new bone at the insertion, fibrosis · prevent → early quadriceps work
- HTO also alters slope and tubercle → harder TKA exposure

#### Low position made at surgery
- TKA errors → **inferior patellar button** · **excess distal femoral cut** → raised joint line
- Quadriceps tendon repair → watch sagittal patellar position → avoids alta or baja

### Management — soft tissue → bone → salvage
- Step 1 → intraoperative **release of tight structures**
- Step 2 → **lower the joint line** → more tibial cut + **distal femoral augment** (Miller)
[[FIG: Fig 14.2 · 14.1
- Step 3 → **tubercle proximalisation** → best for stiff TKA <90° flexion with baja (Miller)
- Native post-traumatic stiffness, Caton index **<0.4** → tubercle proximalisation + open arthrolysis (Campbell)

- Step 4 → **patellectomy**, salvage → shorter quadriceps lever arm, weaker extension

PITFALL — the tibial cut alone
- More tibial cut alone opens both gaps; the line falls only with femoral augments
- Say → "**more tibial cut plus distal femoral augments lowers the joint line**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Judge vs joint line · short tendon vs raised line · release → lower line → tubercle up → patellectomy last**

14.2.l: Arthroplasty — Patella Baja, Stiffness & Periprosthetic Fractures
14.2.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you approach a stiff TKA?"
- "First exclude **infection** → CRP, ESR, aspiration (chapter 6) · then **mechanical** vs **biological** cause."
- "Mechanical (tight gaps, overstuffing, baja) → **revision** · scar only (arthrofibrosis) → lysis."
- "**MUA** (manipulation under anaesthesia) works early → **4–12 weeks**."

### Stiffness vs flexion deformity vs extension lag
- **Stiffness** → arc of motion lost, mainly flexion · stiff TKA = **<90° flexion** (Miller)
- **Flexion deformity** → knee cannot be **passively** extended · balanced TKA → hamstring tightness (Miller)
- **Extension lag** → passive extension full, **active** falls short → quadriceps weakness (Campbell)

### Causes
| Group | Cause | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Tight gaps** | PCL · capsule or gastrocnemius | flexion gap · extension gap |
| **Closure** | tight retinacular closure | less flexion |
| **Patella baja** | low patella | limits flexion |
| **Overstuffed PF** | thick patella · femur in extension | prominent flange, pain |
| **Guarding** | hamstring spasm · infection | protective stiffness |

- Overstuffing → femur placed in extension lifts the anterior profile → chapter 13
- **Arthrofibrosis** → excess scar, no mechanical cause → diagnosis of exclusion

### Management
- **Lysis** (arthroscopic or open) → scar only · **revision** → tight gaps or components
- **MUA** → between **4 and 12 weeks** after primary TKA (Miller)
- Late MUA → periprosthetic fracture, extensor rupture · avoid if femur notched (Campbell)

#### Aftercare that prevents it
- Preoperative flexion deformity → **night splint** → body image returns knee to flexion (Prof Shokry)
- Or pillow under the leg, not the knee · 2 weeks free with walker → physiotherapy

PITFALL — manipulating a mechanical block
- MUA or lysis cannot fix a tight gap, an overstuffed joint or baja
- Say → "**infection out, films for components and gaps, then MUA only for scar**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Infection first · mechanical = revise · scar = lysis · MUA 4–12 weeks · splint the flexed knee at night**

14.3.l: Arthroplasty — Patella Baja, Stiffness & Periprosthetic Fractures
14.3.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "classify and treat a supracondylar fracture above a TKA."
- "Commonest TKA fracture · **0.3–2%** · top of the anterior flange · notching, osteoporosis."
- "**Lewis–Rorabeck** → I undisplaced stable · II displaced stable · III **loose** whatever the displacement."
- "Stable → **locking plate** or **retrograde nail** · loose → **revision** · poor elderly bone → distal femoral replacement."

### Epidemiology & causes
- **Supracondylar femur** → commonest · **0.3–2%** · patella **<1%** · tibia uncommon (Campbell)
- **Anterior flange** top → stress riser on weak supracondylar bone · also an **extended** femoral component
- **Notching** → 30.5% of fractures · less load to failure in cadavers (Campbell)
- Disputed → 1089 TKAs, 30% notched → two fractures, both unnotched (Campbell)

#### Risk & work-up
- Notching, **osteoporosis**, RA (rheumatoid arthritis), steroids, female, revision, neurologic disease
- Injury + old films (± CT) → **component fixation** decides fixation vs revision
- Loose → pain before injury, progressive **lucent lines**, position change on old films

### Classification
| System | Basis | Types |
|---|---|---|
| **Lewis–Rorabeck** | displacement + component | I <5 mm, fixed · II >5 mm, fixed (A simple, B comminuted) · III loose |
| **Su** | level vs proximal flange border | I above · II starts at border, runs up · III extends distal to it |
| **Neer** | displacement only, low yield | 1 <1 cm · 2 >1 cm · 3 >1 cm + comminution |

- **Lewis–Rorabeck** → most important · Type III loose regardless of displacement (Rockwood)
[[FIG: Fig 14.3 · 14.3
- **Su** → I–II nail or plate · III (low) → locking plate or revision (Rockwood)
- None grades **bone stock** → decides revision vs distal femoral replacement

### Prevention
- Old implants → remove, wait ≥**3 months** · same session → **long stem** (Handbook)
- Screw holes = stress risers · centre the cuts · no **eccentric box** in PS or CCK
- **Never notch** · forced or found → stem + protected weight bearing · intraoperative fracture → fix, same sitting

### Management
| Lewis–Rorabeck | Treatment |
|---|---|
| **I** (<5 mm, stable) | conservative · brace, fixation not mandatory |
| **II** (>5 mm, stable) | fixation → locking plate or retrograde nail |
| **III** (loose) | revision → long stem · **distal femoral replacement** (megaprosthesis) |

- Handbook → IIA regular plate, IIB locking plate · nonlocked plates collapse into varus (Rockwood)
- Stable → premolded supracondylar locking plate · submuscular → fewer nonunions (Miller)

#### Plate or nail
- Locked plate vs retrograde nail → similar results · nonunion ≈9% (Rockwood)
[[FIG: Fig 14.4 · 14.3
- **Retrograde nail** → CR or open-box PS · distal fragment must take locking screws
- Closed box, narrow notch, stemmed implant → **high-speed burr** or antegrade nail
- Plate → very distal, comminuted or osteoporotic · indirect reduction, early motion

#### Results, revision & the elderly
- Nails → 13 fractures, **11 (85%)** healed, mean 16 weeks (Campbell) · weak bone → hinged brace
- Fracture at fixation surface or loose femur → **long stem** into diaphysis ± strut allograft
- Old age → high 1-year mortality · comminuted osteoporotic bone → **distal femoral replacement** → immediate weight bearing
- Severe osteoporosis → **allograft-prosthetic composite** → 9 of 10 united (Campbell)

PITFALL — fixing a loose component
- Plate or nail around a loose femoral component fails whatever the displacement
- Say → "**I check fixation on old films first: loose = Rorabeck III = revision**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Flange top · notch disputed · Rorabeck I brace, II plate/nail, III revise · old + poor bone = DFR**

14.4.l: Arthroplasty — Patella Baja, Stiffness & Periprosthetic Fractures
14.4.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "classify tibial and patellar fractures around a TKA."
- "Tibia → **Felix** I plateau · II stem · III distal · IV tubercle → A fixed, B loose, C intraoperative."
- "Patella → extensor mechanism + button fixation decide → **Ortiguera–Berry** I, II, III."
- "Intact extensor, stable button → **conservative** · loose → excise · extensor disrupted → fix."

### Tibial fractures — Felix
| Type | Location | Subtype |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | tibial plateau | **A** component fixed |
| **II** | around the stem (metaphyseal) | **B** component loose |
| **III** | distal to the stem | **C** intraoperative |
| **IV** | tibial tubercle | — |

- Felix → location, implant stability, timing · much rarer than femoral (Rockwood)
[[FIG: Fig 14.5 · 14.4
- Type I plateau → often loose component and varus malalignment

#### Management
- Fixed, undisplaced → **conservative** · fixed, displaced → **fixation** · loose → **long-stem revision**
- **Tubercle** fracture → threatens extensor → tension band · failed → allograft or mesh augment
- Intraoperative (C) → trial or stem impaction → stem bypassing the fracture
- Gunshot case → **offset stem** + proximal screws (Prof Sherief Khaled)
[[FIG: Fig 14.6 · 14.4

### Patellar fractures — classification
| Ortiguera–Berry | Extensor | Button | Bone stock |
|---|---|---|---|
| **I** | intact | well fixed | — |
| **II** | disrupted | fixed or loose | — |
| **IIIa** | intact | loose | reasonable |
| **IIIb** | intact | loose | poor |

- Ortiguera–Berry → most used · Campbell's types without eponym (Rockwood)
- **Goldberg** (Handbook) → 1 peripheral · 2 fixation or extensor · 3 inferior pole · 4 fracture-dislocation
- Risk → excess resection, **lateral release**, maltracking, raised joint line, flexion >**115°** (Campbell)
- Also trauma, PMMA heat necrosis, revision, large central peg · often **asymptomatic** on routine films

### Patellar fractures — management
| Situation (Goldberg) | Treatment |
|---|---|
| **1** · extensor and fixation intact | cylinder cast or immobiliser, 6 weeks |
| **2** · extensor disrupted, button fixed | fixation · transverse → tension band + retinacular repair |
| **2** · button loose | fixation + revision or excision |
| **3B** · tendon intact | conservative |
| **3A** · tendon torn | partial patellectomy + repair |

- No **straight-leg raise** → extensor disrupted → operate
- Loose button → excise, do not replace · poor bone → leave unresurfaced (**patelloplasty**)
- Comminution, poor bone → patellectomy + extensor repair
- Operative types II–III → up to **50%** complications, nonunion, implant failure (Campbell)

#### Lecture case
- Fall at 9 months → crushed patella, extensor intact → fragments out (Prof Sherief Khaled)
[[FIG: Fig 14.7 · 14.4
- No augmentation device in Egypt · 4 and 3.5 years → small remnant, normal gait

PITFALL — operating on every patellar fracture
- Patellar fixation often fails; intact extensor usually does well in a cast
- Say → "**straight-leg raise intact and button stable → nonoperative**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Felix I–IV + A/B/C · Ortiguera I fixed, II extensor, III loose · SLR decides · 50% complications if operated**
